chapter_title: Foundations of Economic Thinking: Incentives and Opportunity Cost

questions.question: If you spend $10 on a movie ticket instead of buying a book, what is the opportunity cost?
options: The book you did not buy
The time spent at the theater
questions.answer: The book you did not buy
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative foregone, which in this case is the book.
questions.flashcard_back: The value of the next best alternative foregone when a decision is made.
questions.flashcard_explanation: It represents the trade-off inherent in every choice due to scarcity.

questions.question: Economic policy is most effective when it focuses on legislative intent rather than human behavior.
questions.explanation: Effective policy must account for how individuals actually respond to incentives, not just the stated goals of the legislation.
questions.flashcard_front: Should policy focus on intent or behavior?
questions.flashcard_back: Policy should focus on human behavior and incentives.
questions.flashcard_explanation: Legislative intent often fails if it ignores how people respond to new incentives.

questions.question: Why might increasing tax rates on high-income earners lead to a decrease in total tax revenue?
questions.answer: High-income earners are mobile and may relocate to jurisdictions with lower taxes, leading to capital flight and a shrinking tax base.
questions.explanation: When the tax burden becomes too high, the incentive to stay is reduced, causing the tax base to shrink faster than the rate increases.
questions.flashcard_front: Why do static tax projections often fail?
questions.flashcard_back: They ignore behavioral changes like capital flight and relocation.
questions.flashcard_explanation: Taxpayers respond to incentives; high rates can cause them to move, reducing the total tax base.
